post.summary: Exchanges a refresh token for a new pair.
post.description:
⚠️ Anonymous by necessity, not by oversight: the access token is expired by
definition when this is called, so requiring one would make the endpoint useless.
The refresh token in the body is the credential.

post.summary: Ends the session the refresh token belongs to.

there is no privilege to escalate in throwing your own credential away. Requiring a
valid access token would mean that signing out stops working at exactly the moment
it matters most: when the session has already expired and the user is trying to
leave a shared machine clean.

delete.summary: Forgets this driver's device. Called on sign out.
delete.description:
Phones are handed over between shifts. Without this, the next driver to sign in on
the same device keeps receiving the previous one's notifications: trips that are
not theirs, on a screen they did not ask for.

get.summary: Inbox of a Raphael.Driver user.
get.description:
Only what is still visible: driver notifications live for twelve hours, one shift, and so do route signals. See `NotificationRetentionPolicy`.
⚠️ Signals included, hence the explicit scope. A route signal is not written for a person to read, but hiding it left the driver with a bell that moved for reasons they could not see. Until we decide what a driver should be told when their route changes underneath them, the honest answer is to show it.
The two rules addressed to a driver are `TRIP_CANCELLED`, only when the trip was already under way, and the `DRIVER_ROUTE_UPDATED` signal, only after Pull-out. An empty list is the normal answer rather than a sign of breakage.

get.summary: How many unread notifications the bell should show.
get.description:
Route signals count, the same rows the inbox above returns. A badge and a list that
disagree about the same screen is worse than either number on its own.

post.summary: Puts one notification back in the unread pile.
post.description:
A driver who opens a notice at the wheel cannot act on it right then. Without a way
back, the only thing keeping it from being lost is their memory.

get.summary: The driver's open request to be called back, if any, and when they may press again.

post.summary: Asks the office to call back, or reminds it if a request is already open.
"I can talk now", after the office tried to call and could not reach the driver.
Sends the driver a real in-app notification: stored, delivered and in their inbox.
post.description:
Not a shortcut through the hub. It writes the notification and its recipient row the same way the engine does, so what comes back is a genuine test of the whole path: the live message, the bell counter, the inbox after a refresh, and view/unview on a recipient id that actually exists.
The response reports how many hub connections the driver has open, which is the first thing worth knowing when a notification does not show up: zero means the app never reached `/hubs/notifications`, and no amount of resending will help.

post.summary: Sends the driver a push through Firebase, carrying the deep link data.
post.description:
Unlike `test-driver-push`, this one needs no token of its own and includes the
extras the app reads to open the notifications page, so it exercises the tap as well
as the delivery. Close the app before calling it: a push that arrives with the app
in the foreground proves less than one that wakes it.

get.summary: Route changes waiting to be acted on. Never notices.
get.description:
A signal says the schedule the app has on screen is out of date. It is delivered live over the hub; this endpoint exists so an app that was closed, or whose socket was down, can drain whatever it missed when it comes back.
This is the signals on their own. `GET notifications` returns them too, mixed with the notices, because the bell shows them today; an app draining what it missed wants only these, and asking for the whole inbox to filter it again would move a server decision back into every client.

delete.summary: Deletes a signal the application has already acted on.
delete.description:
⚠️ Signals only. A notice is refused, and that is the point: a cancellation is a record somebody may have to answer for later, and no driver tidying their screen should be able to destroy one. What a driver does not want to see, the app hides on the device; deleting notices belongs to the retention policy alone.
⚠️ Raphael.Driver stopped calling this. A signal is shown in the bell now, so deleting it the moment the app acted on it would take a row off a list the driver had not read yet. The app remembers on the device which signals it already acted on, and the row ages out on its own. Kept here because it is the only safe way to remove one, and the next client that needs it will need it to exist.

post.summary: Synchronizes multiple trips in a single batch request using Form-Data.
post.description:
This endpoint performs an Upsert (Update or Insert) operation:
  • If the TripId exists for your integrator, the trip is updated.
  • If the TripId does not exist, a new trip is created and linked to your account.
  • Customers are identified by RiderId (or FullName + Phone if RiderId is missing).
  • SpaceTypes and FundingSources are identified by their Name.
  • Attachments: You can upload Word or PDF files for each trip.
Attachment Handling: The 'Attachment' field expects a binary file (PDF or Word). When you upload a file:
  • FileContent: This is the raw binary data of your file. Do not send as Base64; send as a binary part of the multipart form.
  • FileName: Automatically extracted from the uploaded file's metadata.
  • ContentType: Automatically detected (e.g., application/pdf).
Batch Format: For multiple trips, use indexed keys: trips[0].TripId, trips[0].Attachment, trips[1].TripId, etc. Requirement: This endpoint requires multipart/form-data because it handles binary file transfers.

200.description: Every trip in the batch was stored.

207.description: Some trips were stored and some were rejected. See Results.

400.description: The request is empty or contains malformed data.

401.description: Unauthorized. API Key is invalid or missing.

422.description: Every trip in the batch was rejected. See Results.

Do not put the API Key in the URL. It opens your whole integration and would be written to every access log between you and us. That is what this exchange is for.

post.summary: Keeps this notification: the cleanup will never expire or delete it.
post.description:
For a notice somebody will have to answer for later — a trip a patient disputes, a cancellation under investigation. Any signed-in office user can do it, because keeping a record is the safe direction: the cost of an unnecessary archive is a row, and the cost of losing one is a question nobody can answer.
It does not put the notice back in anybody's inbox: the reading window does not move, so it still leaves the office list twelve hours after it was raised.
Note the identifier: this takes the notification id, unlike view and acknowledge, which take the recipient row. Archiving is a decision about the record itself, not about one audience's copy of it.

get.summary: What we already know about a Google place, so the client need not buy it again.
get.description:
⚠️ A `NotFound` here is normal and is not an error: it means nobody has looked this place up yet. Only the browser key has Places enabled, so the caller fetches it and posts the result back to `POST /api/routing/place`. Every dispatcher after that gets it from here for nothing.
Pass `language` — the one Maps was loaded in — here and in the body of the `POST`. Each language is cached apart, so a place bought by a Spanish session never puts "EE. UU." on an English user's trip.

post.summary: Remembers a place the client had to buy from Google.
Records Google calls a client made on its own, so they reach the usage panel.
post.description:
The map pages carry the browser key and talk to Google directly — a map load, an address autocomplete, a geocode when a pin is dragged. This server never sees them, and without this endpoint the panel would be blind to a third of the invoice.
Any signed-in client may report. This writes nothing but counters, and the worst a wrong report can do is make an estimate wrong — which is why the panel marks these SKUs as reported rather than measured. Unknown SKU names are ignored rather than refused: a client one version ahead should not get an error for it.

⚠️ An unknown trip answers 200 with an empty list, not 404. A caller has to be able to tell "this API does not have the endpoint yet" from "this trip has no events", because Desktop falls back to the by-route reader on the first and must not on the second. 404 is reserved for the route not existing.
Born with `[Authorize]` per the ecosystem rule. The rest of this controller is still open — see `_meta/SECURITY_FINDINGS.md` F9 — but that is a separate remediation and closing it here would break whoever calls those without a token.

put.summary: Writes a whole route's new order in one request.
put.description:
Dragging one stop renumbers every stop after it. Sent one by one, that is a round
trip per stop to a database reached over the internet, with the route left partly
renumbered if any of them fails. Here it is one call and one transaction.

get.summary: Tomorrow's schedule for a run, and only tomorrow.
get.description:
Raphael.Driver calls this behind its "Future Schedule" button. The button keeps its name because that is what the driver has always pressed; what it shows is the next day, because everything ahead came back as one list with several Pull-outs and several Pull-ins in it and no way to tell the days apart.
`driver/future` stays as it is. Its name describes what it does, other callers may want it, and renaming an endpoint to mean something narrower is how a client nobody remembered keeps working and starts lying.

get.summary: Everything that has ever been set.
One setting by key.

post.summary: Stores a chunk of a broker's CSV file in one request.
post.description:
Answers per row, so read Results rather than the status code alone: a rejected row stores nothing and does not stop the rest of the chunk. Each carries an ErrorCode, a message saying what to fix in the file, a Retryable flag and a CorrelationId for support.
Re-sending a chunk is safe: rows are matched on the broker's own TripId, so a trip that already went in is updated rather than duplicated. That is what lets the client retry a chunk the shared host refused without the office having to work out which half of the file arrived.

200.description: Every row in the chunk was stored.

207.description: Some rows were stored and some were rejected. See Results.

400.description: The chunk is empty, or names a funding source that does not exist.

422.description: Every row in the chunk was rejected. See Results.

get.summary: The build serving this request, and which environment it is.
get.description:
Anonymous. It publishes the version of our own code, which is a fingerprint, and that
was weighed: the cost is that an attacker learns which build is running, and the
benefit is that every client can check it is current before login and every ticket
can name the build without credentials. Nothing here describes the inside of the
system, and nothing here is patient data.

ApiVersionDetailsDto.title:
Everything needed to answer a support ticket about a deployed API: which build, from
which commit, produced when, against which database schema, and which client versions it
expects.

version.description: The build serving this request, for example `1.4.0`.

commit.description:
Full commit hash this was built from. null in a build that did not
come from CI, which is itself the answer: it was not deployed by the workflow.

builtUtc.description:
When CI produced this build, in UTC. null for the same reason as
Raphael.Shared.DTOs.ApiVersionDetailsDto.Commit.

environment.description: Which environment this is. What `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` says.

apiContract.description:
Version of the OpenAPI document, `v1`. Moves only on a breaking change to the
shape of the API, and so is almost never the answer to "why did this stop working".

integrationContract.description:
Version of `INTEGRATION_API_SPEC.md` this build implements. This is the number
an external integrator codes against.

databaseMigration.description:
Name of the last migration applied to the database this API is connected to, for
example `20260910_AddEarlyArrivalWait`.

minimumClientVersions.description:
Oldest version of each client application this build expects to serve, keyed by the
name the application sends in `X-Client-App`. Advice, not a gate: an older
client is marked in the response and served normally.

ApiVersionDetailsDto.description:
Behind authentication, for the same reason `/health/ready` is: the state of the database and the commit a binary was cut from are facts about the inside of the system, and there is no reason to publish them. The number by itself is public — see Raphael.Shared.DTOs.ApiVersionDto.
Carries no patient data and never will. It is the one page a support engineer is guaranteed to open during an incident, which makes it the worst possible place to put something that must not be pasted into a ticket (CLAUDE.md §3).

ApiVersionDto.title:
The least a caller needs in order to know what it is talking to: which build, and whether
it is production.

version.description:
The build serving this request, for example `1.4.0`. It is the git tag: the
deployment refuses to publish a tag that disagrees with it.

environment.description:
Which environment this is: `Production`, `Development`. What
`ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT` says.

ApiVersionDto.description: Deliberately two fields. This is the one version answer served without a token, so it carries what an application needs before anybody has signed in — to check it is current, and to refuse to show production data on a screen that was pointed at development by mistake — and nothing that describes the inside of the system. The commit, the build time and the state of the database live in Raphael.Shared.DTOs.ApiVersionDetailsDto, behind authentication.

discard the one it sent, or its next renewal presents a token the server has already

indistinguishable from a stolen credential and ends the session.

CatalogIntegrator.description:
This is not an Raphael.Shared.Entities.Integrator. An Integrator is somebody we already work with and who has a key against our API. This is the directory we work the phone from: who they are, where they are, who to ask for. A row is never deleted — when we stop being interested it goes Raphael.Shared.Entities.Catalog.CatalogIntegrator.IsActive false, because the reason we looked at it once is worth keeping.
When an arrangement is reached, the row is added to our company: an Raphael.Shared.Entities.Integrator is created pointing back here through `Integrator.CatalogIntegratorId`, and this row stays exactly where it is. Several providers can add the same entity, each one getting its own Integrator row.

Geocoding is on demand. The source files bring no coordinates, and geocoding the whole
catalog at once is not possible anyway: the Geocoding API allows 1,500 calls a day and the
catalog is thousands of rows. So a row arrives as Raphael.Shared.Entities.Catalog.GeocodeStatus.NotRequested and only moves
when someone asks for it — see MAPS_POLICY.md.

LoginResponseDto.title: What `POST /api/Auth/login` answers with.

token.description: The access token. Sent on every request as `Authorization: Bearer`.

userId.description: A string, not a number. Kept that way because the clients declare it so.

role.description: The role id, as a string. Same reason as Raphael.Shared.DTOs.LoginResponseDto.UserId.

accessTokenExpiresAtUtc.description:
When Raphael.Shared.DTOs.LoginResponseDto.Token stops being accepted. Given plainly so a client does not
have to decode the JWT to find out.

refreshToken.description:
Opaque, single-use, and the only thing that can buy a new access token. Stored by
the client where a credential belongs — DPAPI on Windows, SecureStorage on the
phone — never beside the executable.

refreshTokenExpiresAtUtc.description:
When the refresh token dies if it goes unused. Every use pushes it forward, up to a
ceiling the client is not told about because it cannot do anything with it.

LoginResponseDto.description:
⚠️ This replaced an anonymous object, and every property below is named and typed to serialise to exactly what that object produced — including `userId` and `role` being strings rather than numbers, which is what the clients' own `LoginResponse` classes declare. An anonymous object is not a contract anybody can mirror, which is how three applications came to hold three guesses at this shape.
The three token fields at the bottom are additive. A client that does not know about them deserialises the response into its own class and ignores them, which is why Desktop 1.8.1 and Driver 1.4.0 keep working untouched against this.

ScheduleResequenceRequest.title: A whole route's new order, sent in one piece.
ScheduleResequenceRequest.description:
Dragging one stop renumbers every stop after it, and each of those used to be its own
PUT — against a database that is on the internet, so the dispatcher waited for a round
trip per stop while the grid sat still. This carries the lot in one request and one
transaction, so the route is never half-renumbered.
            
The route and the date travel with it and are not decoration: they are what the server
checks the stops against, so a request cannot renumber stops belonging to another route
or another day.

ScheduleStopSequenceDto.description: One stop's place in the route, and what the router worked out for it.

system: everything else (routes, schedules, billing, notifications) hangs off it.

dropoffPhone.description: Phone number at the drop-off place. PHI.

vehicleRouteId.description: Route the trip is assigned to. Null while it is still unassigned.

Broker, that is, from Raphael.Desktop.

TripImportConflictDto.title: The trip that was already there, when a row is refused for duplicating one.

tripId.description: The broker identifier the existing trip is filed under.

status.description: Where the existing trip has got to, so a started journey is not overwritten.

TripImportConflictDto.description:
"This is a duplicate" is not an answer anybody can act on: the dispatcher has to know
WHICH trip, or they have to go and hunt for it. Duplicate here means the same patient on
the same day between the same two addresses in the same window - so those are the fields,
plus the identifier the existing trip is filed under, which is how it gets found again.

TripImportItemDto.title: One row of a broker's CSV file, already mapped by the desktop app.

tripId.description: The broker's own identifier for the trip. This is what an import is matched on.

date.description: Calendar day of the trip. Any time of day is ignored.

fromTime.description: Pickup time, or null when the file leaves it open.

distance.description: Distance in miles, as the broker states it.

type.description: Appointment or Return. Decided by the client across the whole file.

willCall.description: True when the patient rings to be collected instead of holding a booked hour.

spaceTypeName.description: Short code of the space type: AMB, WCH, STR and the rest.

spaceTypeDescription.description: Used only when the space type has to be created on first sight.

capacityTypeName.description: Capacity the space type counts against, used only when creating it.

riderId.description: The key the patient is matched on. Built by the client when the file has none.

TripImportItemDto.description:
Everything the server needs to store the trip travels in this object, including the patient and the space type, so that a file of four hundred trips costs a handful of requests instead of one per row per lookup.
The shared host reads a burst of requests from one address as an attack and withdraws the permissions of the whole application, which is how an import used to end with the connection dropped and part of the file missing. Batching is not an optimisation here: it is what keeps the import finishing at all.
Names and identifiers rather than foreign keys, deliberately. The desktop app cannot know the id of a patient it has not created yet, and having it ask would put the round trip back that this endpoint exists to remove.

A batch reports per row because a batch fails per row. The office needs to know which
trips did not go in and why, so they can be found in the original file and corrected.

TripImportRequestDto.title: A chunk of a CSV import: the funding source it was filed under, and its rows.

fundingSourceId.description: The funding source chosen on the import screen. It applies to every row.

TripImportRequestDto.description:
The client splits a file into chunks and sends them one after another, never at the
same time. The chunk exists so a request stays inside its timeout and so progress can
be reported, not because of any size limit: a hundred rows measured 171 KB.

success.description: True only when every row in the chunk was stored.

createdCount.description: How many rows were stored as new trips.

updatedCount.description: How many rows overwrote an existing trip.

timestamp.description: When the chunk was processed, in UTC.

results.description: One entry per row received, in the order they were sent.

providerId.description: The Provider carrying out the trip; null when it is the super broker's.

TripTrackingDto.title:
What the Booking Portal's tracking view shows for one trip: where, when it is expected, and
what has already happened.

inProgress.description: True while the vehicle may be shown: driver on the way, at the door, or carrying the patient.

requestedPickupTime.description: The pickup time the clinic booked.

appointmentTime.description: The appointment time the clinic booked.

pickupArrivedAt.description: When the driver reached the pickup.

pickedUpAt.description: When the patient got on board.

droppedOffAt.description: When the patient was left at the destination.

externalTripId.description: The trip's own number (the integrator's id), shown as "Trip #40233". Null when it has none.

customerName.description: The patient, for the page's title. The same name the clinic's trip list shows.

distance.description: Road miles of the trip, as routed.

pickupPlace.description: The places' names ("Home", "Sunrise Dialysis Center"), when the trip has them.

pickupPhone.description: The phone to call about the pickup: the patient's, as booked.

providerName.description: The provider carrying the trip. Null means Raphael's own fleet.

vehicleType.description: The kind of vehicle on the route ("Wheelchair", "Stretcher"), or null before routing.

TripTrackingDto.description:
Times are the business's wall-clock hours of the trip's day, as the route computes them
(TIME_POLICY): shown as they are, never converted. The ETAs are the route's own
(`Schedule.ETATime`), so they cost nothing to read; they are null until the trip is routed.

providerId.description: Provider operating the trip. Null means the broker runs it itself.

providerTimeZoneId.description: The timezone this trip is operated in, as an IANA identifier.

WillCallUpdateDto.title: The pickup time a dispatcher settled on when moving a trip's Will Call state.
WillCallUpdateDto.description:
Only the time travels, because it is the only thing the dispatcher gets to decide: the flag itself, the status and the history row are the server's business.
⚠️ Wall-clock time where the trip is operated, not the hour of the machine that sent it. Null means "let the server use the operation's own clock" — for an activation, now where the trip runs; for the reverse, the 23:59 the office reads as waiting on the patient. See `_meta/TIME_POLICY.md` §2B.

Bearer.description: Paste the token on its own. Swagger adds the "Bearer " prefix.

ApiKey.description: Key of the Customer Service Bot. Sent as 'X-Api-Key'.
ApiKey.name: X-Api-Key

IntegrationApiKey.description: Key of an external integrator, the one on its Integrators row. Sent as 'X-Integration-ApiKey'. It also identifies who is calling: the trips it creates and reads are that integrator's own.
IntegrationApiKey.name: X-Integration-ApiKey
